and artificial intelligence (AI) has seen significant growth in recent times. While AI systems are improving rapidly, they are still far from true intelligence - and it's difficult to know exactly what that means. True intelligence involves natural intelligence, but our understanding of the two is often mistreated as interchangeable concepts. This means that exploring AI through the study of natural intelligence may offer valuable insights into the characteristics of true intelligence. This study examines how computational thinking can serve as a key feature of natural intelligence, and how artificial neural networks can be used to model natural intelligence. By doing so, we also explore the potential for artificial intelligence to emerge from the intersection of natural and artificial intelligence. To achieve this, we develop a computational model of general intelligence (CMG) that is both artificial and natural, and test it using the same set of 10 diverse logic puzzles used by Chinese AI researchers. Our results indicate that CMG is capable of solving these puzzles just like its artificial counterpart - and like the latter, CMG is capable of learning. This study is part of an ongoing research effort that is exploring the relationship between natural, artificial, and computational intelligence. This research is intended to offer a unified view of these interrelated concepts and offer a potential path towards the development of a more general and artificial intelligence. Traditional models are typically based on average outcomes and may not accurately capture rapid fluctuations observed in individual datasets. In this research, mixed effects models are employed to account for consistent and rapid dynamic patterns simultaneously. However, as individual-specific coefficients become a parameter in the model, estimation difficulties and high variability in the data render traditional software solvable (if at all) extremely challenging, limiting analysis to smaller datasets. In response, an optimized version of the mixed effects models is presented, using a 2-stage factorial Gaussian-Hermite quadrature to transform the model and generate more efficient estimators using all available data. This optimized model is implemented in R as a package 'ageDynamic'. In this research, we also discuss how Age-specific rates of infection can be effectively estimated using the model and how Infection Rate Dynamics can be reliably modeled without being confounded by variables that are consistent over time. Various model checks are presented to ensure the optimized model is computationally efficient, flexible, and suitable for use with real-world data sets. Finally, we illustrate the capabilities of the optimized model using individual-level data on infectious processes. This is a crucial development as there have been relatively few studies on modeling Age-specific rates of infection and Infection Rate Dynamics jointly. In addition, individual-level data on infectious processes often suffer from low visibility due to being a 'blind' outcome of other processes, making it a new and interesting dynamic that may have applications in fields of digital health. Using data from before, during, and after pandemics on 'greenberry', a mobile app tracking users' positive COVID test and self-reported Infection Free Days, we demonstrate the optimized model can effectively estimate key health outcomes and Infection Rate Dynamics, offer valuable public health insights, and inform the development of digital health interventions. This is a first-of-its-kind study combining insights from Public Health, TTI reports, and digital health data, and a new frontier in the study of health dynamics. With the growing advancements in the collection of digital health data that describes individuals' behaviors over time, this research has significant implications for understanding, preventing, and managing the spread of infectious diseases as it may create new opportunities for early detection, intervention, and digital health innovation. Finally, in this research, we also provide the optimal analytic tools for exploring digital health data at an individual level. To fully leverage existing data, a novel method referred to as data augmentation by inheritance has been developed to generate new classes from parent classes through various techniques, such as splitting or merging, of these parent classes. The method splits a class into two or more children or merges a class with another one, then uses a parent class detector trained on data of the parent classes and applies it to the child classes. Because the child classes inherit all training data features from their parent classes, a detector trained on the parent classes, a well-established phenomenon in the field known as the pre-trained knowledge transfer method, is expected to also work well on the child classes. Experimental results from an open-source object detection system have shown that this method successfully migrates knowledge from a parent to child classes without the need for re-training. The method was successfully tested using the MS-COCO and VOC datasets. The approach addresses a major limitation in using existing data hierarchies and was incorporated into an open-source object detection system to study its impact. Overall results have shown a significant improvement in detecting rare and uncommon object classes without increasing the amount of training data. Due to this method's ability to generate a large number of new classes from existing ones, we have been able to test the performance of the system on a very large extended version of the MS-COCO dataset containing many rare and uncommon object classes. The method has the potential to leverage existing data to train detectors for a wide range of object classes. The data augmentation by inheritance method has the potential to facilitate the development of detectors for a very broad range of object classes. For instance, existing data on vehicles, then using this data to train detectors for all other object classes without the need for substantial new data. To fully evaluate the potential of the method, an extended version of the MS-COCO dataset has been created by adding many rare and uncommon object classes. These classes are then split into children or merged with other classes to create a new data hierarchy. The open-source object detection system has been trained on parent class detectors trained on MS-COCO, then tested on child classes of the parent classes. Experimental results have shown a significant improvement in detecting the broad range of object classes without increasing the amount of training data. The data augmentation by inheritance method has the potential to fully leverage existing data to meet the needs of detection tasks, including identifying all object classes in an extended version of the MS-COCO dataset

However, little attention has been given to how the process of preprocessing data affects the outcome of clustering. A common data preprocessing method that has gained significant attention is the one conducted within the framework of information-geometric learning. This method utilizes Riemannian manifold-based operations to realize mappings that are well-suited to the data at hand, ensuring that the information structure within the data remains intact during preprocessing. 

  To address how this method impacts clustering, we compared the performance of preprocessing conducted on raw data versus Riemannian-structured data on a range of real-world datasets. Notably, the comparison showed that using the Riemannian-structured preprocessing generally leads to better results for clustering, although the benefit is more pronounced in larger datasets. A similar trend was observed when we analyzed the effect of Riemannian-structured preprocessing on the convergence of clustering algorithms: it facilitates convergence to better-quality clusters in both real-world datasets and synthetic data arranged in distinct structural patterns. 

  To understand the underlying reason for the better performance of Riemannian-structured preprocessing, we analyzed the effect of using sufficient anchoring in the Riemannian manifold-based learning approach. We discovered that using sufficient anchoring generally results in worse clustering outcomes or requires a more comprehensive dataset to yield better results. Additionally, the findings indicated that in cases where there are no class labels available, the benefit of using the Riemannian-structured preprocessing is more clearly attributed to the within-class structure within the data. 

  Based on the results of this study, we arrived at several key conclusions. First, sufficient anchoring does not necessarily contribute to better clustering performance. Second, the benefit of using the Riemannian-structured preprocessing appears to be more clearly attributed to the within-class structure in the absence of available class labels. Therefore, an alternative approach to achieving this structure through feature learning or a probabilistic model may yield improved clustering results. 

  Finally, an important question remains whether the benefit of using the Riemannian-structured preprocessing can be further harnessed in other applications of data clustering. We propose that integrating clustering with sufficient anchoring and within-class structure is a promising area for further exploration and may ultimately yield better outcome in the future.

Initially, a bounding value for the optimal solution is established through the probabilistic approach, while selecting variables are integrated into both the objective function and constraint equations in the form of linear and convex terms. The use of ranking loss as a method to incorporate knowledge into the recommendation is gaining traction, with numerous strategies having been developed to incorporate knowledge through low rank constraints. However, the fundamental question - to what extent does incorporating knowledge through ranking impact recommendation accuracy? - remains largely unanswered, as existing studies have primarily focused on exploring different knowledge incorporation methods rather than the inherent properties of ranking loss. Traditional CUDA implementations face difficulties in achieving high GPU occupancy, resulting in the limitation of being able to handle larger networks on a single GPU. This paper presents an innovative, flexible framework designed to overcome these challenges, allowing sequences of smaller threads to collaboratively use the resources of a GPU quickly and efficiently. This new approach is model-agnostic, implying that any type of neural network can be seamlessly integrated with the existing CUDA infrastructure, or the more recent oneNF framework, without requiring significant modifications. By embracing this flexible model-agnostic solution, the new framework is capable of significantly surpassing the capabilities of other collaborative approaches, particularly in terms of enabling larger networks to be trained on a single GPU. However, voxel-based statistics are not suitable for capturing spatial heterogeneity within and between scans, nor do they address the issue of voxel dropout caused by signal loss or lesions growing out of bounds. To overcome these challenges, we propose a graphical model-based approach that utilizes a Bayesian inference framework to make predictions and predictions intervals for data analysis. Through simulations and real-world multiple sclerosis data analysis experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, showing improved predictive accuracy and data analysis outcomes compared to existing voxel-based statistics techniques. Notably, we find that a significant proportion of voxels (on average ~55%) are non-stable across a single patient's scan sequence, underscoring the necessity of our proposed analysis framework for accurate data analysis. The advantages of our method are illustrated through case studies of data analysis. These findings highlight the significance of incorporating both spatial and temporal complexities in multiple sclerosis data analysis. The proposed graphical model-based approach is suitable for a wide range of neurological data types and can be extended for use in various neurological disease studies, including both individual subject analysis and group comparisons. The implementation of this method is available online through the github repository https://github.com/MILAB-SystemsBiology/MSGraphicalModel/tree/main/MSGraphicalModel. To date, the results show promising outcomes for the analysis of advanced multiple sclerosis data. Nevertheless, further studies are required to fully investigate the effects of varying clinical stages on the predictive accuracy of these methods. Our main objective is to test the capabilities of gradient-enhanced machine learning methods to facilitate condensed matter physics research. We utilized the restricted Born Oppenheimer approximation and a machine learning algorithm to model the quantum dynamics of the Heisenberg model in the X-Y-Z framework on a two-dimensional square lattice. Conversely, we observed that the model performs suboptimal if gradients are not used, resulting in highly disparate outcomes in thermal properties such as the quantum dynamic susceptibility. Our study offers a competitive approach that combines first-principle principles and machine learning to fully model quantum many-body systems. It presents opportunities for future research in quantum dynamics, quantum dynamics of quantum fluids, and quantum dynamics of tunneling effects. Despite significant advancements in generating dense masks for an entire image, these methods are often unreliable due to the inherent noise present in unsupervised data.  Most existing unsupervised techniques focus primarily on predicting the classes of an image's contents rather than creating accurate masks.  To address this challenge, we propose the Use Adversarial Segmentation Tasks method, which uses a combination of multiple tasks to improve the performance of semantic segmentation tasks. These pipelines can automatically convert a repository's content into a testable environment for developers, a feature known as "try it".  A recent study aimed to determine the extent to which developers in the Python community take advantage of this feature, and what factors contribute to its adoption.  The study, which analyzed nearly 300,000 GitHub repositories and 120,000 CI/CD pipelines, identified key indicators that predict the use of "try it" pipelines in the first and second stages of the development process. A subsequent survey of 150 developers, repository owners, and GitHub users helped to clarify the study's findings, revealing that the desire for fast feedback and improved code quality drive the adoption of"try it" pipelines in the first stage of the development process, while second-stage adoption is motivated by the need for feedback on code transformations and resource utilization.  The findings can contribute to the improvement of CI/CD pipelines and"try it" pipelines, promoting feedback loops and code quality, ultimately leading to a better user experience for GitHub repository owners. This occurs when there is no actual difference in the percentages being compared. To address this problem, we've created a R package called innocentpie. Traditional non-equilibrium statistical mechanics approaches often rely on systems with discrete conservation laws, like particle number, or predefined conserved quantities. Nevertheless, transportation systems, such as those influenced by external electric or gravitational forces, are more accurately described as continuous systems. These systems are difficult to analyze using traditional methods, which is why we have developed a new approach based on response theory to study particle transport through a continuous system without a well-defined conservation law. By focusing on non-equilibrium single-file transport and using response theory, we have successfully derived an expression for the number of particles transported as a function of the system's discrete and continuous energy cost. This transport analysis was performed using the Metropolis algorithm, which allowed us to validate our findings by demonstrating a significant correlation between the probability distribution of transported particles and the system's cumulative energy cost. Moreover, by applying an exact solution to the Fokker-Planck equation, we have discovered that the system's confinement affects particle transport statistics. These discoveries highlight the system's out-of-equilibrium nature, where both energy constraints and the system's size influence the probability distribution of transported particles. Lastly, by examining single-file transport under varying electric field intensities, we have observed periodic patterns in the system's confinement effect, which correlates with previous findings on discrete systems, thus validating our approach. These results not only contribute to a deeper understanding of particle transport through a continuous system without a well-defined conservation law but also pave the way for future investigations into the effects of system confinement on particle flow. Furthermore, the methodology employed in this work can serve as a framework for analyzing transportation systems, such as those influenced by external electric or gravitational forces, where the system's energy constraints must be carefully considered. This paper explores an innovative method of increasing a CNN's capacity while maintaining its compact size by incorporating a Sliding Integrated Kernel (SIK) structure. This new structure allows smaller feature maps to learn through the incorporation of multiple filters with shared parameters across various spatial locations. As a result, the total number of parameters and model size remain unchanged. Unlike previous studies, where a growth rate was required for large models, SIK can augment any existing CNN with a reduced number of parameters, thereby remedy the requirement for intricate architectures or a large dataset in training. If nerve fibers are viewed as interconnected dielectric breakdown points within an electric field, the observed anomalies can be resolved through a simple statistical mechanism. This mechanism is based on the standard principles of fluid flow and dielectric relaxation. When electric force is applied to the dielectric, solid conduction paths form, and as current increases, the channels shrink due to further dielectric saturation. When the dielectric is relieved of charge, these channels dissipate, only to reform when the dielectric returns to equilibrium. This process accounts for the observed fluctuations in conduction, temperature dependence, and saturation thresholds. It also provides a plausible explanation for the observed fluctuations in membrane thickness. Furthermore, it can be projected that an abrupt change in conduction properties, similar to a phase transition, is possible near the temperature at which water becomes unstable. This could result in the observed loss of conduction, and it is suggested that this critical temperature is approximately 21 Celsius, which is near the temperature at which fish are most active. When nerve fibers are subjected to high frequencies of current, the dielectric relaxation mechanism predicts that conduction will suffer from memory loss due to rapid and continuous remodeling of the channels. This effect could impair high-frequency processing in the nervous system. The model also suggests that slower dielectric relaxation mechanisms could contribute to the phenomenon of temporal summation. Overall, it appears that the difficult conduction properties of giant squid axons can be resolved by employing the simplest of modeling assumptions. To account for this uncertainty when computing particle tracking transport, multiple numerical simulations are typically run and their results averaged. This paper investigates whether uncertainty quantification methods can be used to accurately account for the uncertainty in these simulations. Specifically, we explore the use of such methods in two types of problems: one where the path of a particle is calculated assuming it is fully dissolved, and another where the particle remains solid. Our results show that uncertainty quantification methods can indeed provide a reliable estimate for the average transport of particles, validated against the average results of multiple simulations. and cognitive science, heavily relied upon in classical AI, yet largely still a research topic within the field of machine learning and artificial intelligence. Previous attempts to develop a system to resolve this challenge have either only learned to replicate data encoded in a specific format, or preserve accuracy when handling new data using continuous representations. The effectiveness of a system's representation is typically assessed by measuring its ability to predict its own future encoding patterns or those of similar data. While successful in predicting representations of similar data, these models often fall short in predicting their own future encodings. We propose a new approach, continuous and semi-continuous representation, where a portion of the data is encoded in a specific format and the rest in a continuous format. We suggest that this mixed representation is the natural state and thus inevitable. Furthermore, we argue that resolving the representation problem can be achieved by identifying the 'divide' where the classical code transitions into the continuous format. We introduce a method, 'encodings as graphs,' to visually present and analyze the representations within a system, helping to identify the point at which the representation switches from a structured to unstructured format. Lastly, we describe different scenarios where experts might need to intervene in order to pinpoint the correct representation boundary. Our work is inspired by the cognitive sciences' interest in understanding the human ability to comprehend and represent information. We demonstrate how our method can be used to analyze and understand a model of human vision developed by the computer scientist and neurobiologist, Harnad. The model is shown to have a natural representation, and we identify the point where this representation's structure transitions into a continuous format. Moreover, we embed this model in a graph, revealing its representation evolution, and confirming its accuracy by matching the original model's accuracy in predicting its own future encodings. Overall, our new approach to the representation problem is effective, and we show that semi-continuous representations are both inevitable and efficient. Ultimately, we conclude that the representation problem is a paradigm problem that is likely to remain an active area of research within the field of artificial intelligence and machine learning. This work is inspired by the vibrant community of researchers focusing on understanding the human ability to comprehend and represent information, at the intersection of artificial intelligence, machine learning, cognitive science, and data science. The full paper on this topic can be found at https://research.laurencedadler.com/publications

Initially, we analyzed various forms of Distillation methods, categorizing them into two groups: those that utilize data and those that utilize tasks. Next, we identified two critical criteria for the practical application of Distillation methods: the first is to ensure the training of the teacher model is completed and the second is to ensure the trained teacher model can effectively guide the student model. To address these two limitations, we introduced the concepts of Cross-Distillation methods and Task-Distillation methods. One Cross-Distillation method utilized the images of the teacher model and the student model in the same environment and achieved improved performance by over 9%, and Task-Distillation methods enabled the student model to perform better on task-specific test data by over 11%. The outcomes of this study demonstrate that combining Distillation methods is a vital strategy for further improving their performance. Additionally, cross-distillation methods offer advantages not previously seen in single-distillation methods or combinations of distinct models, and therefore, can be a valuable direction for future research in this area. an intricate issue that researchers have grappled with for centuries. Although there have been numerous attempts to measure values such as cooperation and fairness using experimental methods, these studies typically focus on a specific aspect and are also typically confined to a laboratory setting, limiting their scope. We have developed an comprehensive and scalable framework to assess these values in real-world societies by analyzing their responses to two manipulations:  how members are selected for a task, and how rewards are shared in a collaboration scenario.  Using this framework, we have analyzed responses from over 2,000 individuals across 12 societies, including a diverse range of cultures, and discovered a consistent pattern in how these values are positioned relative to each other.  Interestingly, we have found that these values can be distinct from what people say they value when asked through surveys. Moreover, we have found connections between these values and various metrics that describe social behavior, as well as connections to personality traits and economic indicators such as GDP.  These findings highlight the significance of considering the complex web of values that exist in a society, rather than relying on individual opinions, in order to gain a deeper understanding.  Furthermore, we have found that these values can provide predictive insights into the stability of societies, with their relationships being stronger in more stable societies.  Ultimately, this framework can be used to track the development and changes in a society's value system over time.  Furthermore, it also suggests that these values can be influenced by external interventions, such as social policies, in order to steer the society towards a more stable course, if desired.  In the accompanying code repository, we have provided the raw data and the code used for the analysis, enabling others to reproduce the results.  Furthermore, we have included additional analysis that were not included in the paper, in order to facilitate future research in this area, including a study on whether these values can be linked to historical data.  In the future, this framework can be used to investigate the causal effects of specific interventions, such as policy changes, on a society's value system, in order to identify the most effective strategies to improve relationships between these values, if desired.  Ultimately, this framework can be used to improve our understanding of human nature and the complex web of values that exist in a society, rather than simply being a collection of separate individual values. We explore the mathematical concepts of graph assembly and inversion, along with the complexities associated with these problems from a computational standpoint. We provide evidence to support the idea that determining whether a graph can be fully reconstructed through interaction is an NP-complete task. Considering the potential of an intelligent agent to mimic biological processes, this research also investigates how applicable NP-completeness is in models of genetic evolution. We demonstrate that assembly and inversion are essentially equivalent to combinatorial search, establishing a connection to well-known problems in artificial intelligence. We prove that the reversal of a graph (wherein each edge is flipped) can be computationally complex, yet show that this reversal is equivalent to a reasoning task that is known to be challenging for artificial intelligence systems, and further, that this system can be simulated by a computational model of interaction that is widely accepted as a realistic model of genetic evolution. We conclude that the reversal of a graph is complex because it is a form of interleaved path finding, where standard approaches to artificial intelligence are often ineffective in solving this problem. We also show that the reversal of a graph is essentially equivalent to a form of interaction in a computational model that describes the exchange of messages between agents, demonstrating the complexity of this interaction. We use this interaction as a foundation for additional complexity results in graph assembly and inversion, showing that various forms of interaction are necessarily complex when the goal is to produce a specified subgraph, and that these results are unaffected by the nature of the graph model when the goal of interaction is to assemble or reverse the graph. Furthermore, we illustrate the practical implications of these complexity results by applying them to three distinct models of genetic evolution that are rooted in these interaction models, showing that three distinct evolutionary algorithms are necessarily complex as well. We use these complexity results to provide a lower bound on the number of generations required by any evolutionary algorithm that aims to solve the reversal problem. We argue that these complexity results have significant implications for the design of algorithms for reversing graphs, and that these consequences are significant because reversing graphs is a fundamental problem in discrete mathematics that has far-reaching applications in multiple fields, and that the problem has attracted the attention of researchers from a variety of disciplinary backgrounds. Specifically, translating machine learning models learned from coloured images to black and white images poses an interesting problem as it involves modelling the relationship between a image's visual properties and its relevance to a human observer. In this work, we investigate this connection and introduce an innovative approach to expand the scope of this translation task using an image's subjective appeal as the source domain. We then propose ColourlessNET, a two-part neural network capable of learning and reversing the process of adding or removing colour from an image. We test this network on various tasks including translating coloured, black and white, and stylized images into new categories, demonstrating its capabilities and versatility. Notably, this network also performs well on its reverse operation, successfully recreating images that have undergone a process of being rendered in black and white. We analyze the implications of pre-training the network on image preference data and identify situations in which this approach leads to novel and unexpected results, exemplifying the potential of incorporating human perception into neural network models. Lastly, we outline the broader significance of this research, suggesting its potential to develop neural networks that mirror human perception directly. We present a new line of research into a neutral network that learns to learn from human perception and demonstrates the potential for a neural network to resemble human perception laid out in the accompanying thesis. We present a new task that appears underexplored: developing a neutral network that learns to learn from human perception. We show that our neutral network is capable of efficiently learning this complex relationship at a speed several orders of magnitude higher than other approaches. In particular, we investigate the use of image preference data for training a neural network that accurately describes an image's visual properties. We identify that this relationship is often misleading and easily manipulated, prompting us to reframe this task as a process of deconstructing an image's visual properties in a way that is both concise and universally applicable. We propose this new task as a more suitable approach to the original problem. We then investigate how this relationship could be inferred using data from image preferences, revealing that this correlation is often artificial and easily manipulated. In response, we redefine the scope of this relationship as an exercise in discovering the underlying structure of an image's visual properties in a way that is both universally applicable and minimally descriptive. We employ the image preference data to develop and test this new approach to translating images, outperforming traditional methods on various tasks as measured by the recently established Image Cropping Challenge

However, standard reinforcement learning methods often require massive training datasets and can result in unpredictable, noisy outputs due to their maximization-based approach, whereas segmentation tasks typically benefit from minimization. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a novel method that leverages the power of generative adversarial networks, specifically the energy-based model, to impose a prior on the representation space underpining the segmentation model. By maximizing a surrogate gradient estimate of the segmentation energy based on the class probabilities, we achieve a strong and stable segmentation model that excels in few-shot environments and boasts consistent, high-quality outputs. Experimentally, our approach significantly surpasses existing alternatives in terms of COCO-SEG mIoU evaluation, boasting up to 10% greater accuracy than baseline models, and remarkably, our model is even robust in the absence of additional data for only a singular sample, matching the performance of models with access to substantial extra training data. Moreover, our model's segmentation output is of notably higher quality than the baseline, resulting in improved boundary detection, and we find that this improvement is directly linked to the optimisation of an energy-based model of the representation space. Finally, we explore the potential of our model as a active object-centred model, focussing on building object classes from scratch. Our results show that this approach results in the model learning object masks which are of higher quality than baseline, and we anticipate that this represents a promising direction for further investigation. The code used to support this research is available upon request. The specific dataset generated to support this research cannot be publicly shared due to its size, however we anticipate that our approach could be further developed to support more general object-centred learning. The findings of this research demonstrate a promising step towards the creation of active object-centred learning, and we anticipate that this could be further optimised through the integration of further techniques, such as future interactions and an expanded learning paradigm. The greatest challenge to further integrating such improvements would be the need to re-design the reward signal to better align with the specific requirements of the task, and balancing this with the requirement to maintain task coherence in the data generated. One potential solution could be to establish coherent sub-sets of the data, and to develop the reward based on this segmentation to better ensure that the model learns a meaningful representation. The exploration of further integrations such as this, and the potential for further automation of computer vision tasks, will be explored in future research

These efficient technologies can support high-performance neural networks, but often come with notable drawbacks such as inaccurate sensor data and unreliable hardware patterns. Despite extensive research in neuroscience and neurophysics, the mechanisms driving hardware imperfections remain understudied in the field. In this investigation, we delve into the root causes of hardware errors and model their effects on spiking neural networks, revealing how imperfections can sometimes act as features rather than bugs. To showcase this, we develop and test ECHO, an energy-efficient Spiking Neural Network (SNN) crossbar chip that purposefully introduces hardware glitches as a proof-of-concept. By combining both proactive bug introduction and automatic error compensation through adaptation, we establish a unique framework for enhancing model resilience. Static glitch insertion causes a decrease in performance for majority vote-based SNNs, but also introduces opportunities for improved results through selective glitch placement. However, while glitch compensation sometimes results in restored original performance, it also may result in introduction of new noise stability limits. We observed that chip temperature significantly influences hardware performance, often outperforming best-effort SNN implementation on the same silicon. This implies that controlled introduction of hardware glitches can serve as data representation, effectively functioning as circuit-level features that enhance model capabilities. By exploring the effects of hardware errors and imperfections on neural microcircuitry and developing both bug-introducing and error-compensating technologies, we gain a deeper understanding of the complex interactions between circuit and software architects, material scientists, and the ever-adaptable biological models inspiring these systems. As such platforms bridge the gaps in performance, reliability, and efficiency, we may uncover new avenues for innovation at the intersection of circuit and neurobiology. Ultimately, by integrating hardware glitches as functional units, we may succeed in achieving the Holy Grail of neuromorphic computing – a cyber-physical system capable of withstanding damage. The source code and simulator model supporting this research are available on GitHub at https://github.com/Algebra7/ECHO-SNN. This paper proposes an innovative framework, referred to as CurBS, which regulates the level of exchange of information among parallel tasks and restricts mutual influences, thus minimizing performance overlap among tasks. CurBS is an extension of the Bi-Realistic Cyclic Optimizer (RECO) and is characterized by several key enhancements: a modified architecture to facilitate a balanced information flow among tasks; a new curriculum learning approach to regulate the exchange of information among tasks; and an adaptive adjustment of influences from mutual interactions. CurBS is demonstrated on multiple datasets across various domains including multi-label classification, multi-view image alignment, hate speech detection, and music genre classification. The results show that CurBS successfully controls collaborative knowledge sharing and reduces performance overlap among tasks. Moreover, CurBS outperforms other models on multiple performance metrics, notably the state-of-the-art MTOR, on various datasets with little or no information exchange. Additionally, the results show that CurBS enhances the prediction accuracy and robustness of individual tasks. From another perspective, CurBS facilitates a stable and consistent ranking of performances for each task. This work will support the development of collaborative deep learning models with enhanced stability and robustness for individual tasks. The source code of CurBS is available at https://github.com/ghassenjl/CurBS. quantum circuits has become a critical area of focus.  A key concept, known as quantum circuit complexity, essentially measures how challenging it is to approximate the output distribution of a quantum circuit using a set of quantum operations and states.  This paper examines various aspects of complexity influenced by different types of noises present in quantum systems.  It's been discovered that introducing a specific form of noise into a quantum circuit effectively increases its complexity in a linear manner.  Additionally, our findings illustrate that certain noise models act as 'barriers' preventing lower-dimensional circuits from achieving higher-dimensional ones, even if there's a significant difference in the circuit dimensions.  Importantly, our results are independent of circuit depth but rather relate to the horizontal distance between unitary channels.  Studying how non-degenerate noise affects quantum circuits has also uncovered some surprising insights.  It's been found, for instance, that two parallel layers of a mixed noise model can't be distinguished from a single layer using a specific set of quantum resources.  This complexity influence has been shown to extend to certain classes of quantum circuits, including those computing complex functions and those that remain stable under specific errors.  Overall, our research has significant implications for understanding the efficiency of classical and quantum algorithms.  These findings may even hold relevance for other complexity measures, such as quantum communication complexity.  As an example, our study has shown that a specific type of non-local entanglement acts as a 'flag' for identifying certain types of complex functions computed by quantum circuits.  This complexity influence could have far-reaching consequences for various areas of quantum information theory.  Conversely, our results on the impact of local noise in mixed noise models have shown that some of these effects don't necessarily affect the efficiency of functions computed by quantum circuits.  This complexity influence could have particular implications for certain classes of local operations and, as a result, may not be significant for certain areas of quantum information theory.  Despite these differences, our research on the impact of noise on quantum circuits has significant implications for understanding the efficiency of classical and quantum algorithms.  This complexity influence could have particular consequences for certain areas of quantum information theory, particularly those involving communication complexity.  To illustrate this point, our study has shown that a specific type of complex function can be easily solved using a quantum circuit of moderate depth but is challenging to solve using classical algorithms.  However, our research has also shown that a certain level of local noise can make it difficult to approximate the output distribution of the quantum circuit using a set of quantum operations and states

Since objective metrics often fail to align with subjective evaluations, researchers continue to seek a universal metric that correlates with human perception.  Deep learning approaches have shown more flexibility in incorporating subjective evaluations, and this paper investigates their effectiveness in predicting overall IQA scores in comparison to traditional metrics like structural similarity index magnitude and mean squared error.  Although deep learning models can capture complex image characteristics, they are limited by their reliance on large amounts of annotated data.  Since these models are not feasible for content with unknown quality, we propose a multi-stage framework that begins with a pre-trained deep learning model and an ordinary differentiable function to produce a quality-aware content representation.  This representation is then used to produce a quality estimate through a different deep learning model.  Our framework can also utilize subjective evaluations to identify the most accurate representations, enabling it to produce higher quality estimates than alternative approaches.  Results show that this framework produces near state-of-the-art quality estimates when trained with comprehensive datasets, and achieves impressive performance when applied to content with unknown quality using limited reference content.  Furthermore, the content representation learned by our framework exhibits resilience to intense image manipulation, and can serve as a universal metric for evaluating complex images.  Our framework's code and pre-trained models will be made available upon request. Using three distinct methods to simulate neighbor adaptation, we reveal diverse motion patterns and propose a novel theoretical framework that incorporates the concept of variable following distances. We also provide analytical solutions to model two-dimensional movement patterns observed from the simulations. These outcomes may inspire novel approaches for developing multi-robot systems that mimic the agility and sophistication of living collective movement patterns.

The study involved inducing $^7$Li into a thick target at 2.4 MeV/$A$ and transferring its charge to $^9$Be, which led to the investigation of excitation energies above the $5/2^+$ and $7/2^+$ thresholds. By employing high-efficiency germanium arrays, the team studied the response of both targets to delayed $\gamma$-rays. The data revealed distinct, time-resolved resonances at energies approximately 11.2, 11.7, and 12.7 MeV above the $^7$Li + $^9$Be system energy, alongside other broader structures. The calculated half-lives of these observed resonances allowed the identification of two quasi-cluster structures: the $^7$Li-$\alpha$ and the $^7$Li-$\alpha$-neutron. The properties of this novel $^7$Li-$\alpha$-neutron structure were determined, which consists of a $5/2^+$ ground state with an energy threshold of approximately 12.7 MeV and a strong $2^+$ component in its magnetic strength function. The observed strength in this energy range cannot be accounted for by theoretical models. The data suggest that the measured structures are related to the isovector d-wave component observed in the electric dipole radiation of exotic dineutrons. Furthermore, the absence of theoretical models to explain the observed data indicates that dineutron cluster states may persist at higher energies than currently predicted. In contrast, the observed data at energies around 11.2 and 11.7 MeV can be partially accounted for by coupled reaction channels. However, the lack of compatibility in the coupled-channel parameters highlights that the coupled reaction models are still incomplete for these types of reactions. However, their performance is hindered by the time-consuming process of generating predictive distributions. Several studies have sought to expedite the creation of NNE predictions by trading accuracy for speed, yet these efforts have not been grounded in a comprehensive study of trade-offs between accuracy and speed. deep learning architectures in forecasting the short-term evolution of traffic patterns. Specifically, we examine the feasibility of using deep learning models to predict future traffic levels from a current snapshot, particularly useful for informing intelligent decision-making in vehicle-related systems. To this end, we evaluate three distinct models - a conditional random field, a conditional random walk, and a conditional random walk with a memory component - all of which are formulated as point process models. Our results demonstrate that these models can attain an accuracy of 90% with minimal information from past traffic data. Moreover, we have devised a new deep learning framework that can forecast traffic patterns several steps ahead. Our experiments demonstrate that this model can predict traffic levels up to 35 steps in advance with relatively low error margins, particularly for moderate traffic levels. Ultimately, we have established the potential of using deep learning models to forecast the dynamics of traffic, which could potentially expand the horizon of vehicle-related systems to anticipate future events. This could in turn facilitate more effective decision-making, such as suggesting drivers to avoid congested roads to avoid collisions. Furthermore, these models could be modified to detect anomalies in traffic patterns and minimize false alarms. Additional avenues for improvement and research are also identified. The data and source code are publicly available for reference at: https://github.com/kundajelab/traffic-prediction.}, \noindent The present study explores the capabilities of advanced deep learning architectures in forecasting the short-term evolution of traffic patterns. Specifically, we examine the feasibility of using deep learning models to predict future traffic levels from a current snapshot, particularly useful for informing intelligent decision-making in vehicle-related systems. To this end, we evaluate three distinct models - a conditional random field, a conditional random walk, and a conditional random walk with a memory component - all of which are formulated as point process models. Our results demonstrate that these models can predict traffic patterns one step ahead with high accuracy but with diminishing returns for more steps. To circumvent this issue, we have devised a new deep learning framework that can forecast traffic patterns several steps in advance while maintaining low error margins. Our experiments showed that this model can predict traffic levels up to 35 steps in advance with high accuracy. This new model is enabled by using the outputs of the previous models to remember past traffic levels. Moreover, we have discovered that the new model is able to forecast the dynamics of traffic with high accuracy while minimizing errors for more extreme traffic patterns. Our results demonstrate that the new model is able to detect anomalies in traffic patterns while using only minimal information from past traffic data

When performing Bayesian model selection, one's understanding of competing models and their likelihoods determines the value of new data. A unified framework for assessing the information gained from generating synthetic data has been developed in this research, where the value of new data is measured by how effectively it distinguishes between competing models using a specific function known as discrepancy. Initial findings show that the linear discrepancy is directly related to the highest-order linear eigenvalue of a model discrepancy matrix. As a result, this discovery allows for the calculation of the maximum potential learning gained from a set of pre-existing data. Moreover, incorporating the results of Frequentist-based model criticism using generalized linear tests into the Bayesian framework for calculating the value of new data has been explored. This research demonstrates the effectiveness of combining multiple approaches for assessing the information gained. Finally, this research shows that results from the Frequentist framework provide an upper bound on the value of new data and that combining different model likelihoods can produce a more conservative yet accurate estimate of learning gain compared to using highly informative priors in the Bayesian framework. A practical case study of assessing learning gained from imaging data in various resolutions is used to validate and illustrate the proposed framework. As a result, this research presents a unified tool for evaluating learning gained from an experiment's results and provides insights for designers of experiments. Deep learning models have achieved significant success in these domains, and we aim to improve upon their efficiency using channel-perturbation, a novel data augmentation technique that involves minor modifications to input images. Additionally, we propose the use of local patches over sliding windows for feature extraction in place recognition and object detection tasks, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach using a lightweight CNN architecture. Meanwhile, for visual odometry in cluttered scenes, we find that existing methods are inefficient due to reliance on heavy neural networks and extensive data storage. Again, we apply channel-perturbation to generate a large, diverse dataset from minimal original images, and successfully deploy this method in combination with existing object-based visual odometry systems. The resulting models significantly outperform their original counterparts in terms of accuracy and model size, and even surpass some competing approaches in terms of accuracy. Notably, our contributions extend beyond pure academic research to also explore practical applications, such as reducing a smartphone's memory and computational requirements without compromising the quality of RGB-D-based cognitive functions it performs. Finally, our findings on the evaluation datasets indicate that our approach consistently enhances the performance of various state-of-the-art methods in our target domains, and we have made our source code and datasets available for further evaluation and analysis. The deep transfer learning technique is gaining traction as a key strategy in this context. In this study, a general framework is presented that outlines four essential steps for leveraging deep transfer learning for semi-supervised learning. Each sequence is examined in depth, exposing the intricacies often overlooked in current literature. The challenge of converging on optimal solutions in a time-sensitive environment is also addressed. Finally, we suggest perspectives and future research directions to mitigate the limitations of deep transfer learning. Furthermore, we establish a comprehensive comparison of various deep transfer learning approaches in the context of semi-supervised learning for tabular data, highlighting key performance metrics and highlighting promising prospects for future growth. The framework developed here is highly versatile and can be easily adapted to other applications of deep transfer learning. The implementation of this study's framework, along with supporting code, can be accessed at the GitHub repository https://github.com/DaniKeil/DTL-SSL. The code used for this study is based on the Python language and utilizes the TensorFlow platform, along with popular deep learning libraries such as Keras and Pytorch, and widely adopted utility libraries such as NumPy, SciPy, and Scikit-image. The project was reviewed and approved by the institutional review board, ensuring compliance with ethical standards. The approach explored here integrates elements from active learning and deep transfer learning to optimize the training process, reducing reliance on manual labeling. The performance of this hybrid strategy was evaluated through a series of experiments on synthetic data, highlighting its potential to alleviate the reliance on fully labelled datasets. The project's broader implications were also considered, paving the way for future research in this area. The increasing adoption of deep learning in industries has resulted in the widespread use of deep neural networks. However, these networks often require massive amounts of labelled data to produce reliable predictions, leading to the need for more innovative solutions. The Incub8 framework for deep transfer learning for semi-supervised learning for tabular data, presented in this study, is an important innovation in this area, allowing the integration of inductive biases to accelerate learning and converge on optimal solutions significantly faster, even with a much lower number of labelled data. The framework also facilitates the application of concepts from active learning, enabling the automatic identification and focusing on the most challenging cases, further accelerating the convergence process. The framework developed here is an extension of the more general framework outlined in [Keil2019], and is an important contribution to the field

Our findings show that after rearrangement, the process converges uniformly to Poisson point process at any desired rate regardless of the block sizes or their overlapping configuration. These results have significant implications for understanding spatial patterns in biological studies such as cell distributions. Our work provides real-world applications in the context of cell research. We conduct a simulation study to showcase the application of our findings in the context of cell research using R and Rcpp. We also derive a method to estimate the total number of cells based on a finite sample of the process and establish the conditions under which these estimators would converge to the target value.   Our analysis applies the popular Information Need Difficulty (IND) metric, initially designed for evaluating IR systems, but modified for greater alignment with user experiences.   The decision to introduce a policy is typically motivated by the expectation that it will enhance specific aspects, such as reducing costs, improving performance, or ensuring fairness.
  However, little research has been conducted to validate whether these assumptions hold true in practice.
  In this study, we designed a methodology to evaluate the impact of a policy's impact and identified a systematic approach to analyzing the effects of a policy using real-world data.
  The methodology was applied to examine how a policy affecting a system's scalability influenced the performance and resource usage of a distributed application running on a cloud.
  The results showed that the policy had the intended effect on the job duration but did not impact the resource consumption as predicted.
  The paper discusses the challenges encountered in validating assumptions about public policy after deployment.
  This corresponding case study is reprinted from the 11th International Conference on Autonomic Management, held in June 2021. 
  The paper expands on the research originally presented at that event by exploring conceptual and methodological issues related to validating assumptions about public policy after deployment.
  The paper begins by identifying basic requirements for such validation and then discusses specific challenges that may arise in different contexts.
  The research was conducted using the Grid'5000 experimental platform, a community-driven, public infrastructure for distributed systems research, located at five universities across France. 
  The platform consists of a combined fleet of servers, storage systems, and high-performance computing equipment with over 7,000 nodes.
  Access to the platform is granted through a Gantt chart-based resource manager, allowing users to schedule experiments subject to community-defined rules. 
  As part of this study, we conducted two community-organized experiments to validate assumptions about public policy after deployment.
  The first experiment examined the impact of a policy affecting a system's scalability using real-world data from Grid'5000's resources.
  The second experiment explored the impact of a role-based access control policy on users' behavior in a Grid'5000 experiment. 
  The results of the experiments showed that (1) increasing the time slot duration resulted in reduced cost without compromising job duration, (2) increased resource availability per user resulted in reduced average job duration and decreased cost, but also increased cost due to increased resource consumption, and (3) increased accessibility to high-performance virtual machines resulted in a higher adoption rate for virtualization in experiments. 
  The study highlights several challenges that may arise in validating assumptions about public policy after deployment.
  The potential consequences of such difficulties are also discussed.

Using the quasi-free non-equilibrium variational Gross-Pitaevskii equation to describe this dynamics, we observe a non-stationary drawdown of the disorder-embedded condensate. This drawdown is driven by the interplay of disorder and dissipation and simultaneously reduces the disorder's impact and adjusts the stationarity of the pure optical lattice condensate. Its rate is dictated by a non-stationary drawdown parameter, influenced by initial conditions, strength of dissipation, and other factors. Upon reaching equilibrium, the disorder-embedded dissipation-embedded condensate mirrors its mean-field counterpart, with signatures of suppressed quantum effects and pre-thermalization observed in quasi-condensation order. However, these findings rely heavily on initial state clean-ness. When the condensate is seeded with entropy, the equilibrium drawdown parameter exhibits significant variations. To describe this scenario adequately, we propose an extension of the quasi-free non-equilibrium Gross-Pitaevskii model. This model is grounded in a non-equilibrium extension of the Helfand-Zanardi commutator of fluctuations and utilizes an entropy map to track the growth of initial entropy in the condensate. Its predictions align with numerical simulations, underscoring the central role of initial conditions in non-equilibrium many-body physics. Despite multiple-body effects, the drawdown parameter still displays a non-abelian character. This finding opens the door to exploring non-equilibrium quantum Hall states in synthetic and cold atoms lattices. Furthermore, the drawdown parameter serves as a sensitive tool to investigate initial state quality in cold atoms, analogous to diagnostic tools in spin resonance and Bell inequalities. If implemented experimentally, the drawdown parameter could potentially be employed for conditional preparation of a pure initial state, leveraging the ideas of quantum erasure and backward in time causality. Ultimately, the drawdown parameter holds potential to expand the realm of conditional quantum control in cold atoms via non-equilibrium, Helfand-Zanardi driven transformations. The model comprises spins of length one with fixed individual orientations, denoted as $\uparrow$, $\circ$, and $\downarrow$, and interacts via the standard Ising and Heisenberg models, while its symmetry is reduced by the imposed constraint that the arrangement of circular spins must remain uniform in two-dimensional planes. The presence of long-lived, random, zero-sublattice-energy states, which could arise from the inherent inhomogeneities in the spin arrangement, might contribute to the observed discrepancies in the temperature dependencies. The findings indicate that the spin arrangement significantly influences the thermodynamic properties of the composite spin system. The model might serve as a suitable candidate for experimenting with magnetic scattering in quantum Hall systems. Ultimately, the entropy of the system displays a maximum at the phase transition and continues to increase in the paramagnetic phase. Our study aims to assess the clinical safety of report generation models once they have been trained to generate radiology reports. Our evaluation focused specifically on determining if the reports contain clinically accurate and clinically-safe information for patients. Our clinical assessment of the models was carried out by examining (1) diagnostic accuracy, (2) presence of medical specialties, (3) presence of patient identifiers, (4) presence of sensitive language, and (5) language complexity. Our study revealed that existing models are susceptible to producing reports containing diagnostic errors, language from medical specialties, and sensitive content as well as reports that include patient identifiers which could compromise the privacy of patients. Our results also showed that these models produce reports that are less simple and easier to comprehend compared to those written by radiologists. In an effort to minimize these risks, we propose a simple revision to the models to reduce the errors that exist in the data used to train them. We explore the feasibility of identifying eligible individuals who are most in need through government programs, using the government's knowledge as an effective tool. This topic is illustrated through a case study on malaria treatment in Ghana, where we examine the issue of whether to offer free malaria treatment to pregnant women, taking into account that only some women are pregnant and thus in need of the service. This study draws upon a real-world study from the government of Ghana. These studies, including the one on malaria treatment, suggest that a cost-benefit analysis may not always accurately lead to an optimal outcome, as the focus on reducing costs via insurance often comes at the cost of reduced social welfare. This phenomenon is known as the "Malaria Equilibrium". In these settings, graph convolutional networks often feature pooling layers that take into consideration the various graph structures to determine output features. This work presents a framework that formalizes how pooling in graph convolutional networks is utilized to capture significant graph patterns. Two fundamental principles of neural network design are defined: the first ensures unique output features from each layer to circumvent ambiguity during the aggregation process, and the second leverages graph structure to generate these features. This framework is later utilized to develop a new graph convolutional network, described in Section 5.2. Two distinct approaches are defined to implement unique output features from each layer: the first employs a linear transformation with respect to an affinity matrix, and the second utilizes non-linear mapping with respect to an affinity matrix. Both methods are examined in the context of a binary classification task on a undirected, unweighted graph, and the results illustrate how distinct features are produced using the defined transformation. This work is compatible with a broader class of graph convolutional networks that utilize non-linear mapping, as shown in Figure 7. In conclusion, the non-linear feature mapping formulation of graph convolutional networks is defined as a realization of the formalized framework. This is demonstrated in Theorem 4.1. Moreover, the proposed graph convolutional network is compatible with diverse graph types, such as directed graphs and weighted graphs, as shown in Section 5.3. In the future, the impact of unique output features from each layer will be more thoroughly investigated in the context of graph-based neural network design. Graph convolutional networks with varying levels of sparsity, such as sparse networks, sparsity-regularized networks, and sparse-trained networks, will also be examined from the perspective of unique output features from each layer. In addition, the notion of distinct features from each layer is analogous to the concept of disentailment in the realm of graphical models, which seeks to separate underlying variables from observed data. This is a subject for further study in the context of graph-based learning. Lastly, unique output features from each layer are, in fact, a subset of a broader class of features that capture the inherent, discrete structure of a graph. standard phylogenetic network, with the added requirement that it must adhere to
a specific condition - when its levels are arranged in ascending order, each node

intends to explore the resilience of Phylogenetic Networks, specifically their
ability to withstand deletions. More specifically, we aim to identify the least
number of edges required to transform an existing phylogenetic network into a
Persistent one, or alternatively, demonstrate a scenario where no such
transformation is possible even with multiple deletions. This inquiry is crucial
for understanding a broader question: Can any phylogenetic network be converted
into a Persistent one. This very question is the central focus of the second
part of this thesis. Ultimately, we aim to resolve this inquiry affirmatively,
providing a step-by-step operational guide on how to accomplish this conversion
process. This thesis will further investigate the inverse operation - the
reverse-Persistent phylogenetic network transformation, exploring its practical
applications in the field of phylogenetic network metrics and their optimization
problems. This operation, when feasible, essentially serves as a form of 'correction'
function, aimed at removing level inconsistencies while maintaining network
consistency. This concept is closely related to the notion of a Partial Residual
Network, which we will rigorously define and study in the course of our inquiry.
The ability to efficiently and effectively perform the reverse-Persistent network
conversion remains largely unexplored in the existing scientific literature,
despite its potential to deliver a range of benefits and improvements in the
field of phylogenetic network handling and operations. This thesis will focus
on resolving two interconnected but distinct inquiries - the feasibility of
this reverse-Persistent network transformation and the characteristics of the
resulting Residual Network - the Reverse-Persistent Phylogenetic Network (RP-PN)
and its Parallel-Pairwise version (RP3-PN). This is a critical and relatively
unexplored area of the phylogenetic network domain, which this research will
delve into in greater detail. Ultimately, we aim to identify specific
conditions, separability and coterminability, that would allow RP-PN and RP3-PN
to be effectively and efficiently reduced to a simpler form, while also exploring
the inverse operation - the reverse-Persistent network transformation process,

The high cost of training, time constraints, and the need for fast iteration all pose significant challenges. This paper introduces a novel approach to training models called adaptive training, which allows for the creation of multiple small models that mimic a larger, high-capacity model. By creating these smaller models in real-time and training them to perform tasks more efficiently, the approach is able to achieve similar performance at a significantly reduced cost, capitalizing on growing computational power and data availability. A four-task experiment in continuous reinforcement learning found that the adaptive training method could reduce model size by up to 75% and training time by up to 90% compared to traditional methods, while also showcasing its potential to lower costs and increase overall performance. The approach was successfully tested on a range of complex multi-task, continuous reinforcement learning scenarios and was found to outperform both random search and fixed-size models, supporting its claim that it can yield superior results. A detailed analysis of the adaptation process found that the models developed through adaptive training have several appealing characteristics, including a compact structure and time-sensitive training preferences. By understanding these attributes, it is possible to explain the observed performance improvements and guide future research in this area. A theoretical examination of the adaptive training approach found that the variety of models developed through this method are subject to a range of challenges, including inconsistent task representations, variability in both structure and performance, and the potential for models to become over-fitted or redundant. However, the practical implementation of the phase-matching protocol poses significant challenges due to its high sensitivity to laser frequency fluctuations. This paper presents an improved phase-matching QKD implementation using a specially designed phase compensation module (PCM) that dynamically adjusts the frequency of the phase-modulated laser source in real-time. The PCM, which utilizes the fast rotating frequency of an optical diode as a reference, accurately detects and compensates phase fluctuations caused by the diode's light emission. The resulting no-communication and collective attacks can be detected using the partial entanglement swapping method. Our experimental outcomes demonstrate that the proposed PCM is highly effective in reducing the phase shift caused by environmental changes. The combined use of the PCM and the real-time detection method enables a high-data-rate phase-matching QKD implementation with a key exchange rate of around 37.9 bits. This achievement marks a significant step towards the practical implementation of phase-matching QKD in real-world settings, particularly in data transmission scenarios where high-speed communications are crucial. The proposed PCM can also be applied in other phase-based QKD systems to enhance its practical implementation capabilities. Furthermore, the fast-adjusting capability of the diode's light frequency allows for precise compensation of wavefront distortions in optical systems, making the diode itself a potential source of phase randomness when in an unpredictable state. Moreover, the design of the PCM is compatible with fiber-based phase compensation, thereby enabling the development of a high-speed phase-matching QKD implementation that utilizes either bulk optical or fiber-based phase reconstruction methods to achieve a high-data-rate phase-matching QKD at around or above 39.4 megabits per second. Finally, the proposed PCM can be utilized in combination with the partial entanglement swapping method to achieve a high-speed phase-matching QKD implementation through the subkeys of two unbalanced interferometers in a real-time, fiber-based system. Consequently, the combined use of the phase-matching and partial entanglement swapping methods enables the secure construction of a high-speed communication network, enabling the conditional creation of multiple secure channels between any two phases-matching stations based on the detection of a no-communication attack in one link, thus enabling a logical unbreakable cipher in the other links. The traditional approach to MTS typically begins by generating multiple translated sentences using a machine translation system, and then selects the best choice by employing a controller. Our innovation is to apply a probabilistic machine translation (PMT) framework that produces a continuous range of translation possibilities, allowing us to use a cutting-edge classifier as an efficient alternative to choose the most suitable sentence. The good thing about our method is its compatibility with any machine translation system, and we also present a new method to train the PMT model. This study defines and develops a new ontology for characterizing communication protocols in IoT systems. The resulting ontology enhances clarity and facilitates its application in various roles. 

  To test its effectiveness, the ontology was applied to a real-world IoT system through a comparative analysis of the available documentation with and without ontology-based characterization. Additionally, the potential benefits and obstacles of applying this ontology in diverse domains and scopes are discussed.

in internet advertising, which involves displaying relevant advertisements to consumers based on the content of the webpage they are visiting. To boost revenue, online marketplaces have developed real-time bidding (RTB) systems. These systems allow advertisers to set bids for impressions and the ad with the highest bid is prioritized. Nonetheless, issues arise with unbalanced bidding, where faster response times are favored but poor quality ads are more likely to be displayed. To address this, the concept of asynchronous public auction is introduced for sponsored search in this paper, where the bidding process is decoupled from other tasks. This enables a more balanced approach, prioritizing both fast and accurate ad delivery. Specifically, the proposed system consists of a waiting queue to prevent overbearing bidding and a re-run option for events completed in under a millisecond to ensure a fair and effective bidding process. Simulation results show that this asynchronous model outperforms the traditional synchronous model in both response time and ad quality metrics. To achieve this, the proposed system is applied to a real-world scenario, a mobile website providing content in English, and the results demonstrate the benefits of asynchronous model for sponsored search in terms of improved response time and ad quality. Furthermore, the revenue of this system is comparable to the traditional synchronous model. Extensive parameters testing was conducted to verify the effectiveness of this system. Results show that this system is compatible with various asynchronous public auction formats. Finally, the proposed system is ready for commercial integration according to the results of comparison with traditional synchronous model. A stable matching is created by combining two agents in each acceptable pair, resulting in a stable roommates configuration. The goal is to determine if such a matching exists, especially one that maximizes the total roommates by finding an assignment where every agent has a roommate. Our study presents an O(m^n) algorithm to solve this problem, where m is the number of agents and n is the maximum number of elements in each preference list. The algorithm combines elements of complement reduction, especially the rule-based version of Schaefer's isomorphism test, and a Turing machine algorithm to check for Thomsen's graph isomorphism. The latter can be solved in O(m^n) time. The former, when applied to the Stable Roommates problem, can prove the NP-completeness under polynomial time reduction from the Unique Sources problem. Additionally, by modifying this algorithm and using polynomial time computability of Boolean satisfiability in degree two, we can prove the NP-in\-of\-f\-lower\ complexity of the Stable Roommates problem. The same reduction and transformation can also be applied to the Unique Games problem, resulting in the derivation of an NP-complete variant. The latter, when modified and combined with a linear time algorithm for checking Thomsen's graph isomorphism in three vertices, we can prove the NP-completeness of the Unique Games $(m, \epsilon)$-label covering problem. The label 0 in this problem refers to an assignment where every agent has a roommate. Our study also presents an O(m) time algorithm to check if a given assignment is indeed a stable roommates configuration by verifying if the resulting roommates configuration contains no cycles. The algorithm can prove the non-existence of such configurations in the case of odd cycle free graphs and also allows for the derivation of an O(m) time algorithm for finding the minimum degree Thomsen graphs with no cycles. The latter, when combined with a polynomial time algorithm for computing the distance two norm, we can prove the polynomial time computability of the minimum degree Thomsen graphs with no cycles and a minimum edge count of at least four.
