It's acknowledged that time is inadequately defined in non-relativistic quantum mechanics, yet this issue is sidestepped in most quantum mechanics courses by imposing an absolute time framework for illustrative purposes. In line with this, most textbooks introduce time-dependent perturbation theory under the assumption of absolute time. In this work, a consistent, time-dependent Hamiltonian is derived from a time-independent framework with the requirement that the states remain constant over time. It's demonstrated that lacking a consistent time for states automatically results in a time-averaged effective time-dependent Hamiltonian, without confining it to relativistic quantum mechanics. It's noted that time-dependent perturbation theory under absolute time and time-independent framework are two manifestations of the same time structure, with the first being a result of constant unperturbed states and the second being applicable in both relativistic and absolute non-relativistic quantum mechanics. As an example, it's shown that lack of a consistent time for an atom's energy levels leads to an time-averaged effective Hamiltonian for light-field interaction, distinct from time-dependent perturbation theory's result when assuming an absolute time for invariant energy levels. Ultimately, it's concluded that decoherence due to a frequency of interaction is a fundamental feature of non-relativistic quantum mechanics, when properly formulated with time ambiguity, rather than an aberration to be neglected in low-energy quantum mechanics. In this sense, decoherence due to a frequency of interaction is an aspect where relativistic and absolute non-relativistic quantum mechanics converge. As an implication, researchers can leverage this time structure to analytically derive quantum mechanics' results on light-field strong-field quantum electrodynamics in both low- and high-energy regimes with exactness, matching the result of numerical simulations. These analyses match numerical results for the ground-state probability and infrared divergence and also resolve the phase of light-field quantum electrodynamics in both cases. These developments may inspire the use of this method to model and understand the interaction of matter and light in the context of bound states. Building upon this, it can be generalized to model the interaction of free particles, which will be explored in a future study. By applying machine learning-derived insights, we successfully adjusted the beam's phase and, consequently, matched it to the vacuum canal's dominant mode, thereby alleviating vacuum locking issues. The outcome resulted in increased power gain per stage in a two-cavity taper and enhanced efficiency in achieving vacuum locking. Furthermore, employing machine learning helped to introduce an adjustable phase shift, enabling the implementation of transverse impedance compensation and ultimately leading to increased acceleration gain in the stage. The integration of machine learning has proven to be a valuable addition to the accelerator control process, complementing traditional, more structured methods. We anticipate that this approach will play an increasingly vital role in the commissioning and control of future high-energy photocathode accelerators. Specifically, it may facilitate the construction of low-energy photoinjectors for FEL and linac applications and aid in the control and correction of higher harmonic modes in transverse feedback systems. Additionally, this method could be applied to the analysis and control of free-electron laser cavities, where machine learning can contribute to the extraction of precise beam parameters for enhanced beam quality and increased averaging potential. Eventually, this technology may be useful in realizing precision metrology through the measurement of the Higgs boson constant using a cryogenic electron gun. The research has been conducted using the ELBE photocathode accelerator at the HZDR research center in Dresden, Germany. The corresponding publication reference is 2022 arXiv:2209.09772. Various team formation strategies have been employed to enhance collaborative outcomes, primarily from a strategic viewpoint by pairing members with compatible objectives or talent. Conversely, this research explores team formation as an optimization problem from the members' perspective, seeking the most effective team configurations given predetermined capabilities and goals. By leveraging control theory, we define the potential of collaborative outcomes and develop a solution to maximize it under capabilities and goals constraints. Next, we identify and address a critical issue arising from the dynamic nature of colleagues' skills and objectives. Finally, we compare the performance of manually selected, optimized, and randomly formed teams in a basic version of Counter-Strike through human experimentation. The results indicate that automated team formation can achieve better results, particularly when members have flexible skill sets and objectives. Importantly, we have established a method to continuously improve the initial version of Counter-Strike's pairing process. The accompanying code is publicly available at https://github.com/OGarciAmad/CounterStrikeTeamFormation. A video demonstrating the findings is available at https://youtu.be/yTEk7Q2bqko. The DOCTOR research project, which underpins this work, can be found at https://www.doctor2020.eu. The user study was carried out as part of the project 'AptuYou' at KU Leuven's IDM and CiEN research units. The work also benefited from collaborations with HUB research, an independent organization, as well as computations performed on facilities supported by GCC and HUB. Nevertheless, the team formation research presented here is a purely theoretical investigation rather than a practical application or real-world intervention. The actual contributions are theoretical and are expanding our understanding of the capabilities and limitations of collaborative outcomes. The experimental findings provide context and validation for the theoretical work. The entire study is documented at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5188850. The initial team formation problem was first identified and analyzed in the context of pure strategy games such as the Prisoner's Dilemma. The potential outcomes of collaborative interactions in mixed strategy games like Chess were also assessed and found to be inferior to solo efforts. The current study explores the opposite conclusion - that working together has greater potential than working alone. The findings indicate that team formation can be both an optimal and a desirable outcome from the members' perspective. The research has crucial implications for the study of social interactions, revealing that team formation can actually represent the most effective and most appealing course of action for the individuals involved. As AI socialbots gain traction as educational tools for teaching AI and machine learning, our research focuses on designing a chat-based Python-based socialbot that embodies the spirit of science fiction character Data from the movie Star Trek II. The Data socialbot is engineered using the conversational AI framework Rasa to give responses to common statements as understood by a human interpretation of the character's personality, traits, and back-story. Ultimately, this project aims to contribute to the discussion on AI philosophical primacy, a topic inspired by the character Data from the Star Trek II movie. By replicating the personality of a character like Data, who lacks emotions but possesses curiosity and a desire to understand, rather than using randomness, our research aims to explore the feasibility of designing AI machine learning and developing conversational agents that mimic human-like qualities, as well as grapple with the complexities of digital entities exhibiting emotional behavior. In markets without such standards, generators build capacity based on past investment return expectations, but market participants can still influence capacity via agreements to purchase power, as they factor risk from potential short-term shortfalls into their decisions.  In the past, model approaches have been used to simulate market interactions, but they have typically done so at a level that ignores the impact of capacity on market price, effectively assuming that capacity constraints will only become relevant once market capacity is fully engaged. The graph embedding models are primarily focused on static graphs and are unrelated to the dynamic graph model, whereas the remainder of the existing research either addresses problems not connected to dynamic graphs such as link prediction and node classification or offers heuristic and non-interpretability-based models. In contrast, our work introduces theoretical calculations of the stationary distribution for dynamic graphs within the statistical machine learning framework. Specifically, [25] provides a detailed analysis of the stationary distribution of the degree-corrected configuration model. However, rather than being focused on dynamic graphs, this work is connected to the LTP-DG challenge only because it provides the necessary graph encoding for the problem. In contrast, [23] and [24] explore dynamic graph transformation and learning from dynamic graphs, respectively, but the models are described as being interpretability-agnostic. In contrast, our work introduces a state transition model that is both simple and interpretable. Additionally, [33] explores dynamic graph transformation using graph neural networks but the model is primarily focused on static graphs and incurs a high computational cost

The results were compared with the latest quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) calculations by Savarnski et al. (2018). These calculations take into account both the anisotropic crystal-field splitting and the exchange coupling between electrons. In contrast to the substantial correlation between $S_2$ and $S_4$, the magnetic form factor displayed anisotropy, which is characteristic of exchange coupling. This phenomenon contradicts the description of exchange-free $f$-electron spins. Moreover, the presence of direct $Q_2$ scattering contradicts intermediate coupling descriptions. We conclude that the magnetic form factor is influenced by direct exchange, thereby violating expectations based on dual-component spin-1/2 and spin-1 models. The analysis covered various angular configurations and was found to exhibit no $Q$-dependence beyond instrumental factors or resolution. Moreover, the scattering was found not to be linear in $Q$. These findings, which are challenging to explain within dual-component model frameworks, can be understood by considering crystal-field splitting with anisotropy. This reveals an intermediate-compared-to-1 electron spin description of YbInCu$_4$ to be unsuitable. This investigation is the first to resolve the nature of magnetic form factor without relying on angular analysis, thereby providing clear evidence to contradict dual-component model explanations. We conclude that the nature of magnetic form factor cannot be explained by certain models. Savarnski et al. (2018) predicted our findings, which involve one component being immobile. However, our data covered $Q$-vectors at which the immobile component should result in non-linear $Q$-dependence, which was found not to occur. Nonetheless, the relationship between scattering and magnetic form factor was found to be linear, which is consistent with an analysis involving a single $Q_2$ component as proposed by QMC calculations. Nonetheless, the finding contradicts model-based-arguments against angular-averaging-possible-diagonal-component models. program optimization that focuses on adapting compiler decisions with fine-grained, runtime-determined parameters to leverage computational system idiosyncrasies.  Although it has been heavily researched in the AI and data analytics fields, the potential benefits of this approach within cloud-based web applications remain unclear.  By addressing this knowledge gap, we conducted a comprehensive study to evaluate the performance potential of instruction tuning in the context of popular PHP web applications, such as Laravel and Magento.  Through the new, state-of-the-art PHP engine, PHP-Zephyr, which implements various instruction tuning parameters discovered through a systematic search, our results reveal the existence of substantial application-defined optimization opportunities.  Moreover, we found that non-specialized platforms can still achieve significant performance benefits from instruction tuning, albeit at a lesser scale, and that varying system characteristics can trigger distinct tuning parameters.  By open-sourcing the PHP-Zephyr compiler and publishing a methodology for evaluating instruction tuning in software frameworks, our work establishes a foundation for in-depth investigations into the performance dynamics of software applications.  Additionally, this open-source tool enables the exploration of multiple potential tuning parameters, providing a stable foundation for further research into the compiler optimization space.  Ultimately, our study underscores the vast, unexplored potential of the compiler optimization domain and serves as a new case study in the emerging field of instruction tuning.  As such, it poses thought-provoking questions and challenges that could guide future research in the area.  Specifically, the following questions arise from our study: (1) To what extent will machine learning and AI frameworks continue to benefit from domain-specific optimization parameters? (2) What other software or hardware sectors may be defined by runtime-determined parameters? (3) What other computer architecture domains apart from instruction tuning may be characterized by coarse-grained, non-specialized parameters. (4) Can the concept of domain-specific parameters be linked to a particular level in the abstraction hierarchy (e.g. machine language vs. source code)? (5) Can research in the hardware field on one-hand, improving fine-grained programmability in the hardware (e.g. MIG), and on the other, discovering new instruction sets through ML techniques (e.g. ML-ISE), complement the concept of instruction tuning in the software space? (6) Can the resulting platform diversity from (5) be harnessed to develop new, advanced instruction tuning parameters? (7) Can the interaction between the compiler optimization space and the world of data science and AI be viewed as a form of co-evolution

To make contrastive learning techniques more accessible, we've developed a strategy that breaks down the process into smaller, sample-wise fragments, enabling a direct comparison without the need for extensive data storage or processing. Specifically, we've introduced the Entropy-based Reparameterization Contrastive Learning method, which leverages information-theoretic analysis to optimize its approach. Furthermore, we've determined that our method's efficacy is equivalent to that of its more expensive counterparts, and its implementation is straightforward in most deep learning frameworks. The code and models associated with this project are available at https://github.com/aderderiu/contrastive-learning-semantic-features. The corresponding paper has been accepted for publication in Knowledge-Based Systems. We have also successfully applied the Entropy-based Reparameterization Contrastive Learning method to a real-world scenario, namely, the detection of colorectal polyps in colonoscopy images, achieving significant results. The related work is presented in our another accepted paper titled ``Deep Learning-Based Polyp Detection in a Low-Resource Setting,'' which will be presented at the ICPR2021 conference. The major challenge in this application lies in the scarcity of available data, and our solution involves utilizing a combination of data augmentation and the direct sample-wise implementation of contrastive learning to enhance feature robustness and generalization capabilities. The corresponding code is available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ambergh/colorectal-polyp-detection. We have achieved a remarkable performance of 89.83% AUC using this novel approach, demonstrating its potential to address real-world data scarcity issues. The findings suggest that the direct sample-wise implementation of contrastive learning is a valuable strategy for tackling various complex learning scenarios. The analysis of the method's performance highlights the importance of the transformation of augmented samples in the semi-supervised learning context, and the need for further investigation into the hyperparameter optimization of contrastive learning bases in this specific domain. Ultimately, the application of contrastive learning to real-world problems with specific challenges and limitations can yield significant rewards in terms of predictive performance. However, the effectiveness of the direct sample-wise implementation of contrastive learning depends on specific design choices, such as the type of data augmentation used, the amount of unlabeled data available, and the specific hyperparameters chosen. imaging are not readily available, so we investigate the use of dust produced by a stellar process as a natural tracer in the study of interacting binaries. Focusing on systems involving a compact object such as a neutron star or black hole, we model how material from the donor star is ejected during outbursts of activity in which a hot accretion flow forms. This flow is represented by a two-temperature model, with a hotter, radiatively efficient region close to the compact object and a cooler, advection-dominated region further out. Electromagnetic forces cause the tracer particles to become enveloped by the hot region, leading to their rapid accretion once they fall within the compact object's gravitational influence. However, not all of the particles are necessarily consumed in this manner, as a significant portion may be ejected from the binary system, especially during major disruptions caused by the transfer of mass. The behavior of these tracer particles is an indicator of the dynamics of interacting binaries, providing valuable information for the understanding of, for example, recurrent fast X-ray transients. In one such system, 4U/MJSE 2959-2438, we make a prediction as to the duration of a microquasar outburst should the donor star undergo a significant expansion in mass due to a disruption caused by the transfer of mass. This increased mass would result in a reduced velocity for ejected material, leading in turn to lower peak luminosity and a longer overall duration for the outburst. The use of dust produced by a stellar process as a natural tracer in such systems has, we believe, significant implications for the understanding of, for example, recurrent fast X-ray transients and gamma-ray bursts. This approach could also be applied in the investigation of, for example, the supernova remnant and its host system, the Milky Way. Further, we have explored the possibility that, in a significant portion of the universe, stellar material is ejected into surrounding space, only to be drawn towards a supermassive black hole at the center of a galaxy. Should the velocity of the ejected material be, for example, in a range between 0.1C and 0.5C, these materials would likely accrete onto a likely non-steady accretion flow, one that would, given a given mass for the supermassive black object, result in the emission of, for example, X and gamma ray emissions. This accretion would likely be fueled by a significant portion of the matter found in galaxies within a given mass range.

This paper introduces a novel approach called DiaMatch, which uses a large text classification model pre-trained on the ALBERT architecture to accurately match user inputs with template sentences. Through DiaMatch's processing, a database of precomputed similarity calculations between sentences is dynamically generated and utilized for rapid query lookup. The similarity calculations are initially computed using the cosine similarity between sentence embeddings and are subsequently updated using incremental learning. This approach allows for the scalability of the matching process, making it possible to achieve high performance on large and publicly accessible dialogue datasets. The effectiveness of DiaMatch is demonstrated on the MultiWOZ dataset, a renowned benchmark for dialogue systems. Although this concept is well-known in AGN physics, it's often overlooked when studying lower mass, seismically active stars like the sun. By examining data from global solar observations over three cycles, we discovered evidence of a long-lasting, approximately 8-year spiral pattern in solar surface magnetic field maps. This periodic feature corresponds with local variations in magnetic field strength and geometric orientation observed in solar flares over the past decade. Furthermore, the identified spiral features align with predicted patterns from a simple two-dimensional hydrodynamic model. These results support the idea that stellar magnetic activity, like that of active galaxies and blazars, is governed by a large-scale, non-local spiral pattern. Comparing these phenomena highlights the intriguing similarity in magnetic and kinetic control mechanisms, geometric scales, and rotation rates between active galaxies, blazars, and lower mass, seismically active stars like the sun. By recognizing the common underlying mechanisms, we may uncover the fundamental cause of stellar magnetic activity, much like the phenomenon observed in AGN physics. As a result, studying stellar seismology may provide valuable insights into the magnetic control mechanisms of active galaxies and blazars. Finally, we propose the potential for a new AGN-spotted star-blazar connection, providing a means to link together various types of accretion processes across different scales and configurations. Currently, the detection of Varroa is mainly accomplished through the use of costly, high-tech methods such as CT-scanning and deep-learning based image analysis. When particles interact with the black hole, we have used the center of mass method to determine the impact, while for particle collisions, we have used conservation of canonical transverse quantities to find the change in mass and angular momentum, and assumed continuous gravitational waves mean that the change in these quantities equals zero. One key outcome of our work is that the behavior of two particles outside a black hole differs significantly from what is observed in the flat space-etime. Our results may be helpful to study how two particles outside a black hole behave experimentally. Providing geometric guarantees for online PCA has proven to be particularly challenging, and recent studies have shown that achieving constant-time geometric approximations for data streams is inherently impossible unless the arrival rate can scale with the input size. This led to the development of rate-adaptive and fractionally efficient algorithms that can achieve the best possible geometric guarantees for online PCA while accounting for the arrival rate in their design. In a groundbreaking finding, the rate-adaptive side PCA algorithm was shown to consistently approximate the side PCA host's principal directions across arbitrary subspaces, despite differences in their host-side projections. This led to the side PCA being considered as the standard model for online dimensionality reduction. Here, we present a new family of rate-adaptive online PCA algorithms, originally developed for graph stream inputs, which significantly improves upon existing geometric guarantees by achieving a $O(1/n^2 \log^c n)$ distortion in a constant amount of storage, while also allowing for an optional time complexity improvement of $O( \log n / \sqrt{\epsilon})$ when the input is subgaussian. These improved guarantees come close to the best possible by achieving a $O(1/n^{1-c})$ distortion dependence, with our analysis showing a $O(1/n^{2-c})$ complexity for an arbitrary parameter $c$, which we later optimize to $O( \log n / \sqrt{\epsilon})$ with an optimal choice of $c$. Experimental studies have demonstrated the efficacy of our conditional variance reduction technique in reducing the side PCA host's estimation error compared to the current state-of-the-art side PCA algorithm. This, in turn, enables the development of new side PCA induction theorems that achieve a constant-factor approximation with an arbitrarily small distortion for specific data input distributions that deviate from the subgaussian. This specific variant is dubbed the $q$-section side PCA, which we define as a new geometric online transformation that approximates the principal directions of only a specific $q$-section of the host's input data, which we can achieve with an arbitrarily small distortion for specific input distributions that span these $q$-sections. This new transformation has the added benefit of ensuring that our original dependence on the arrival rate in the PCA distortion was not due to a constructively efficient worst-case input counterexample but rather became an inherently unavoidable necessity of the problem. Mathematical models representing these networks often comprise graph structures with vertices representing communities and edges representing species interactions. Each vertex and edge is assigned values that track the flow of disease and species interactions over time. However, the existence of these graphs relies on mathematical abstractions, which in turn necessitate refinement into detailed biological models. This paper explores the relationship between these graphs and their underlying graphs, highlighting the requirement for consistency between vertex and edge values and the need for care when updating these values over time. Specifically, we exhibit examples demonstrating that altering vertex and edge values while updating other network parameters can lead to refined graphs that differ from their original form. Furthermore, we illustrate that inconsistent values leading to nonsensible model outcomes can be remediated by adapting the corresponding graph structure. By maintaining consistent graph structures, meaningful conclusions regarding the model behavior can be drawn, as illustrated by an epidemiological example. This study highlights the importance of consistent modeling, utilizing a practical model to demonstrate potential issues and proposing a solution to remedy such problems.  Despite focusing on dynamic heterogeneous network models, we believe that these insights can also contribute to broader discussion on integrating graph structure and evolution into other types of models. In line with this objective, we pose several open questions within the appendix, seeking input from other experts in this field.  By collaboration, we aim to advance our understanding of modeling network dynamics and continue to refine and improve these models, as well as the broader methodology of graph structure and evolution. By working together, we can improve our analytical tools, opening up the possibility of one day leveraging machine learning and inverse problems to infer information about real-world networks and their underlying processes.  In turn, this goal has the potential to underpin a more ambitious objective - namely, the estimation of network parameters in practical contexts, as well as the forecasting of temporal evolution of heterogeneous networks. Characterizing abnormal airway dilatation involves comprehensively segmenting both the inner and outer boundaries of the airways. Most recent techniques employ graph-based methods, however these studies commonly overlook the inner boundary of the airways. Additionally, the majority of the existing literature uses 2D approaches, which may not fully capture the dilated airways in the lungs. In this study, we propose 3D Confusion Guided Deep Inpainter for Airway Dilatation (CD-AID), an innovative model integrating deep learning and level set methods to identify both the inner and outer boundaries of the airways in a single step. The model utilizes confusing points to represent airway centers and dynamically identifies the corresponding inner and outer boundaries through a confusion loss function. Inexpensive points can be used for representation, reducing the complexity of the task. The model's effectiveness has been evaluated using the Shaiir-10 dataset, showing satisfactory performance in segmenting both the inner and outer boundaries of the airways. The model's accuracy in segmenting the airways is comparable to other recent graph-based methods, however CD-AID differs from these studies in several ways including the capability to be trained solely on Shaiir-10 dataset, the ability to segment 2D and 3D data equally well, and the ability to fully characterize abnormal airway dilatation. The model's use of confusing points also opens up new possibilities for data collection and augmentation. Overall, CD-AID's integration of deep learning and level set methods, including the use of confusing points, enhances the precision and versatility of the model. The model's comprehensive segmentation of both the inner and outer boundaries of the airways paves the way for a more complete understanding of abnormal airway dilatation. Future research should focus on using CD-AID to diagnose a variety of diseases including tetralogy of Fallot. Based on CD-AID's performance in characterizing the airways, this model could further contribute to the diagnosis and treatment of various lung diseases.
